rules.title: A separate partition exists for /tmp is configured
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-writable directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp directory is world-writable, there is a risk of resource exhaustion if it is not bound to a separate partition. In addition, giving /tmp its own file system allows the administrator to set the noexec mount option, making /tmp useless for an attacker installing executable code. It also prevents an attacker from creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated. Once the program is updated, the hard link is broken and the attacker has their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability is found in the program, the attacker can continue to exploit the known flaw.

rules.title: XD/NX support is enabled
rules.explanation: Recent x86-family processors support the ability to prevent code execution on a per-memory-page basis. On AMD processors this capability is typically called No Execute (NX), and on Intel processors it is called Execute Disable (XD). This capability can help prevent exploitation of buffer overflow vulnerabilities and should be enabled whenever possible. Additional steps must be taken to ensure that this protection is enabled, especially on 32-bit systems. Other processors, such as Itanium and POWER, include such support from the start, and the standard kernel for those platforms supports this feature.
rules.impact: Enabling any feature that can protect against buffer overflow attacks improves system security.

rules.title: The SELinux state is enforcing is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux can be in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing. Enforcing is the recommended default operating mode; in enforcing mode SELinux applies the loaded security policy to the entire system. Permissive - the system acts as if SELinux is applying the loaded security policy, including labeling objects and creating access-denial entries in the logs, but does not actually deny any operations. Although permissive mode is not recommended for production systems, it can be useful for SELinux policy development. Disabled is strongly not recommended; the system not only avoids enforcing the SELinux policy, but also avoids labeling any persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux in the future more difficult.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot time to ensure that the controls it provides are continuously in effect.

rules.scope: sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects && sysctl net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.all\.send_redirects" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/* && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.default\.send_redirects" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: Source routed packets are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: In a network, source routing allows the sender to partially or fully specify the route packets take through the network. Conversely, packets that are not source-routed follow a path determined by routers on the network. In some cases, systems may not be routable or reachable from certain locations (for example, private addresses versus Internet-routable addresses), and source-routed packets would therefore need to be used.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route and net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route to 0 disables the system's acceptance of source-routed packets. If source-routed packets were allowed, they could be used to gain access to the system's private addresses because a route can be specified rather than relying on routing protocols that would not permit that routing.
rules.scope: sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route && sysctl net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.all\.accept_source_route" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/* && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.default\.accept_source_route" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation:
ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and tell your host information for sending packets via an alternate path. This is a way to update your system's routing tables from outside. By setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0, the system will not accept ICMP redirect
messages and therefore will not allow outsiders to update the system's routing tables.
rules.impact: Attackers can use forged ICMP redirect messages to maliciously alter system routing tables and cause them to send packets to the wrong networks and allow captured system packets.
rules.scope: sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects && sysctl net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects && grep net\.ipv4\.conf\.all\.accept_redirects" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/* && grep net\.ipv4\.conf\.default\.accept_redirects" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are similar to ICMP redirects, except that they come from gateways listed in the default gateway list. These gateways are assumed to be known to your system and are likely to be trusted.
rules.impact:
Even known gateways can still be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects to 0 protects the system from routing table
updates from possibly compromised known gateways.
rules.scope: sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects && sysctl net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.all\.secure_redirects" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/* && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.default\.secure_redirects" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: Suspicious packets are logged is configured
rules.explanation: When this feature is enabled, it logs packets with non-routable source addresses in the kernel log.
rules.impact: Enabling this feature and logging these packets allows an administrator to investigate the likelihood that an attacker is sending spoofed packets to the system under investigation.
rules.scope: sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians && sysctl net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.all\.log_martians" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/* && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.default\.log_martians" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: ICMP broadcast requests are ignored is configured
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts to 1 will cause the system to ignore all ICMP echo requests and timestamp requests to broadcast and multicast addresses.
rules.impact:
Accepting ICMP echo requests and timestamps with broadcast or multicast destinations for your network can be used to cause your host to start (or participate in) a Smurf
attack. A Smurf attack is based on an attacker sending a large number of ICMP
messages with a spoofed source address. All hosts that receive this message and respond
will send echo reply messages back to the spoofed address, which is likely not
routable. If many hosts respond to the packets, the volume of traffic on the network can
multiply significantly.

rules.title: Logging of bogus responses by the kernel is prevented is configured
rules.explanation: Setting icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses to 1 prevents the kernel from logging bogus (RFC-1122-incompatible) responses to broadcast frames, preventing file systems from being filled with useless log messages.
rules.impact: Some routers (and some attackers) will send replies that violate RFC-1122 and attempt to fill the log filesystem with a large number of useless error messages.

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 causes the Linux kernel to use reverse-path filtering on a received packet to determine whether the packet is valid. Essentially, with reverse-path filtering, if the return packet would not leave through the same interface from which the corresponding original packet arrived, the packet is dropped (and logged if log_martians is set).
rules.impact: Setting these flags is a good way to deter attackers from sending packets into your system that cannot be answered. However, this feature fails if asymmetric routing is used. That occurs when dynamic routing protocols (BGP, OSPF, etc.) are used on your system. If you use asymmetric routing on your system, you will not be able to enable this feature without breaking routing.
rules.scope: sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter && sysctl net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.all\.rp_filter" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/* && grep "net\.ipv4\.conf\.default\.rp_filter" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: TCP SYN cookies are enabled is configured
rules.explanation: When the tcp_syncookies parameter is set, the kernel will process TCP SYN packets normally until the connection queue is full. At that point the SYN cookie feature is triggered, which does not use the SYN queue. Instead, the kernel simply replies to the SYN with a SYN|ACK, but includes a specially crafted TCP sequence number that encodes the source and destination IP addresses and port numbers, as well as the time the packet was sent. A legitimate connection will send the ACK packet of the three-way handshake with the specially crafted sequence number. This allows the system to verify that it received a valid response to the SYN cookie and to accept the connection even if there is no matching SYN in the queue.
rules.impact:
Attackers use SYN attacks for denial of service; the targeted system receives many SYN packets without completing the three-way handshake. This will quickly
consume slots in the kernel's half-open connection queue and prevent legitimate connections. SYN cookies allow the system to accept valid connections even while it is under a denial-of-service attack.

rules.title: IPv6 router advertisements are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: This setting disables the system's ability to accept IPv6 router advertisements.
rules.impact:
It is recommended that systems not accept router advertisements, as they can be tricked into routing traffic to compromised machines. Setting static routes on the system
(typically a single default route to a trusted router) protects the system from incorrect routes.
rules.scope: sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra && sysctl net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra && grep "net\.ipv6\.conf\.all\.accept_ra" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/* && grep "net\.ipv6\.conf\.default\.accept_ra" /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: DCCP is disabled
rules.explanation:
Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) is a transport-layer protocol that
supports streaming multimedia and telephony. DCCP provides a way to access congestion control without needing to do so at the application layer, but it does not provide unordered delivery.
rules.impact: If the protocol is not required, it is recommended not to install drivers in order to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: SCTP is disabled
rules.explanation:
Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a transport-layer protocol used to
support message exchange with multiple message streams in a single connection. It performs functions similar to TCP and UDP, including features of both: it is message-oriented like UDP and provides reliable sequential message transport with congestion control like TCP.
rules.impact: If the protocol is not used, it is recommended not to load the kernel module and to disable the service to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: RDS is disabled
rules.explanation:
Reliable Datagram Sockets (RDS) is a transport-layer protocol designed to
provide low-latency, high-bandwidth communication between cluster nodes.
rules.impact:
If the protocol is not used, it is recommended not to load the kernel module and to
disable the service to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: TIPC is disabled
rules.explanation:
The Transparent Inter-Process Communication (TIPC) protocol is designed to provide
connectivity between cluster nodes.
rules.impact:
If the protocol is not used, it is recommended not to load the kernel module and to
disable the service to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Iptables is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Iptables is a utility that allows a system administrator to configure tables provided by the Linux kernel firewall, implemented as various Netfilter modules, as well as the chains and rules it stores.
rules.impact: Iptables is required to manage and configure the firewall.
rules.scope: apt list iptables iptables-persistent | grep installed 2>&1

rules.title: Audit logs are not deleted automatically is configured
rules.explanation: Configure the maximum audit log file size. Once the log reaches the maximum size, it is rotated and a new log file is started.
rules.impact: In high-security environments, the benefits of maintaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing audit history.

rules.title: The audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: The max_log_file_action parameter determines how to handle an audit log file that reaches the maximum size. The keep_logs value will rotate logs but never delete old logs.
rules.impact: It is important that an appropriate log file size is defined so that logs do not impact the system and audit data is not lost.

rules.title: The system is shut down when audit logs are full is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon must be configured to halt the system when audit logs are full.
rules.impact: In a high-security context, the benefits of retaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing that history.
rules.scope: grep space_left_action /etc/audit/auditd.conf && grep action_mail_acct /etc/audit/auditd.conf && grep admin_space_left_action /etc/audit/auditd.conf

rules.title: The system is shut down when audit logs are full is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon must be configured to halt the system when audit logs are full.
rules.impact: In a high-security context, the benefits of retaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing that history.
rules.scope: grep space_left_action /etc/audit/auditd.conf && grep action_mail_acct /etc/audit/auditd.conf && grep admin_space_left_action /etc/audit/auditd.conf

rules.title: The system is shut down when audit logs are full is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon must be configured to halt the system when audit logs are full.
rules.impact: In a high-security context, the benefits of retaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing that history.
rules.scope: grep space_left_action /etc/audit/auditd.conf && grep action_mail_acct /etc/audit/auditd.conf && grep admin_space_left_action /etc/audit/auditd.conf

rules.title: The Audit service is enabled
rules.explanation: Enable the auditd daemon to record system events.
rules.impact: Collection of system events provides system administrators with information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled
rules.explanation: If the rsyslog service is not enabled, the system may default to using syslogd or log by other means.
rules.impact: If the rsyslog service is not enabled, the system may default to using syslogd or log by other means.

rules.title: Default rsyslog file permissions are configured
rules.explanation:
Rsyslog will create log files that do not yet exist on the system. This setting controls
which permissions are applied to those newly created files. The $FileCreateMode parameter specifies the file creation mode in which rsyslogd creates new files. If not specified, the value 0644 is used.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that log files have the correct permissions to enable archiving and protection of sensitive data.

rules.title: Rsyslog is configured to send logs to a remote log host
rules.explanation: The rsyslog utility supports sending collected logs to a running remote host or receiving messages from remote hosts, reducing administrative overhead.
rules.impact: Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker obtains root access on the local system, they can forge or delete log data stored locally.

rules.title: Remote rsyslog messages are accepted only for designated host logs is configured
rules.explanation:
By default, rsyslog does not listen for log messages arriving from remote systems.
$ModLoad tells rsyslog to load the imtcp.so module so that it can listen on the network over TCP.
The $InputTCPServerRun option tells rsyslogd to listen on the specified TCP port.
rules.impact: The recommendations in this section ensure that remote log hosts are configured to accept rsyslog data only from hosts in the specified domain, and that systems that are not intended to be used as log hosts do not accept any remote rsyslog messages. This provides protection against spoofed log data and ensures that system administrators review sufficiently complete system log data from a central location.

rules.title: Cron daemon is enabled
rules.explanation: The cron daemon is used to run batch jobs on the system.
rules.impact: Although the system may not have user jobs that need to run, the system has maintenance jobs that may include security monitoring that needs to run. If another task-scheduling method is not used, cron is used to run them and should be enabled and running.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/crontab is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/crontab file is used by cron to manage its own jobs. The commands in this item ensure that root is the user and group owner of the file, and that only the owner can access the file.
rules.impact: This file contains information about which system jobs are executed by cron. Write access to these files may give unprivileged users an opportunity to elevate their privileges. Read access to these files may give users insight into the system jobs that are running on the system and provide them an opportunity to obtain unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.hourly is configured
rules.explanation: This directory contains system cron jobs that are intended to run hourly. Files in this directory cannot be modified with the crontab command; they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the root user and group, preventing unprivileged users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.daily is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.daily directory contains system cron jobs that must be run daily. Files in this directory cannot be modified with the crontab command; they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the root user and group, preventing unprivileged users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.weekly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains system cron jobs that need to run weekly. Files in this directory cannot be modified with the crontab command; instead, they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the root user and group, preventing ordinary users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.monthly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains system cron jobs that need to run weekly. Files in this directory cannot be modified with the crontab command; instead, they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the root user and group, preventing ordinary users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.d is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory contains system cron jobs that should run similarly to hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly jobs from /etc/crontab, but require more granular control of their execution. Files in this directory cannot be modified by the crontab command; instead they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the root user and group, preventing ordinary users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Access to /cron is permitted only for authorized users
rules.explanation: If cron is installed on the system, configure /etc/cron.allow to permit specific users to use these services. If /etc/cron.allow does not exist, /etc/cron.deny is checked. Any user not listed in these files may use cron. After removing the deny file, only users in /etc/cron.allow can use cron.
rules.impact: On many systems, only the system administrator is authorized to schedule cron jobs. Using the cron.allow file to control who can run cron jobs enforces this policy. It is easier to manage an allow list than a deny list. On a deny list, you may add a user ID to the system and forget to add it to the deny files.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file contains configuration specifications for sshd. The command below sets the file owner and group to root.
rules.impact: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file must be protected from unauthorized modification by unprivileged users.

rules.title: SSH version 2 is used is configured
rules.explanation: SSH supports two different incompatible protocols: SSH1 and SSH2. SSH1 was the original protocol and was subject to security problems. SSH2 is more advanced and secure.
rules.impact: SSH v1 is susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks, unlike SSH v2.

rules.title: SSH LogLevel is set to INFO is configured
rules.explanation: The INFO level is the baseline level at which only SSH user logon actions are recorded. In many situations, such as incident response, it is important to determine when a particular user was active on the system. A logoff record can exclude those users who disconnected, which helps narrow the field. The VERBOSE level indicates that logon and logoff actions, as well as the key fingerprint for any SSH key used to log on, will be recorded. This information is important for SSH key management, especially in legacy environments.
rules.impact: SSH provides several logging levels with varying degrees of detail. DEBUG is strongly discouraged except strictly for debugging SSH communications, because it provides so much data that it is difficult to identify important security information. INFO is the baseline level that records only SSH user login activity. In many situations, such as incident response, it is important to determine when a particular user was active on the system. A logout record can eliminate those users who have disconnected, which helps narrow the field.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep loglevel

rules.title: SSH X11 forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: The X11Forwarding parameter provides the ability to tunnel X11 traffic over the connection to enable remote graphical sessions.
rules.impact: Disable X11 forwarding unless there is an operational requirement to use X11 applications directly. There is a small risk that remote X11 servers of users who logged in via SSH with X11 forwarding may be compromised by other users on the X11 server. Note that even if X11 forwarding is disabled, users can always set up their own forwarding servers.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep -i x11forwarding

rules.title: SSH MaxAuthTries is set to 4 or less is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxAuthTries parameter specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts permitted for a single connection. When the login failure counter reaches half of this value, error messages detailing the login failure are written to the system log file.
rules.impact: Setting MaxAuthTries to a low value minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. Although the recommended value is 4, set the number according to site policy.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep maxauthtries

rules.title: SSH IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Setting this parameter requires users to enter a password when authenticating with ssh.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep ignorerhosts

rules.title: SSH HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies whether authentication via trusted hosts through user .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv, together with successful client host public-key authentication, is permitted. This option applies only to SSH protocol version 2.
rules.impact: Even if .rhosts files are ineffective when support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use .rhosts files in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep hostbasedauthentication

rules.title: SSH root login is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitRootLogin parameter specifies whether the root user can log in via ssh. The default is "no".
rules.impact: Disallowing root login via SSH requires system administrators to authenticate using their individual accounts and then escalate to root via sudo or su. This in turn limits the ability to deny authorship and provides a clear audit trail in the event of a security incident.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep permitrootlogin

rules.title: SSH PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitEmptyPasswords parameter specifies whether the SSH server permits authentication with empty password strings.
rules.impact: Denying remote shell access to accounts with an empty password reduces the likelihood of unauthorized access to the system.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep permitemptypasswords

rules.title: SSH PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment parameter allows users to present environment options to the ssh daemon.
rules.impact: Allowing users to set environment variables via the SSH daemon can potentially allow users to bypass security measures (for example, setting an execution path in which ssh executes Trojan programs).
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep permituserenvironment

rules.title: Use only approved MAC algorithms
rules.explanation: This variable restricts the MAC algorithm types that SSH may use during communication.
rules.impact: MD5 algorithms and 96-bit MACs are considered weak and have been shown to increase vulnerability to SSH downgrade attacks. Weak algorithms continue to receive significant attention as a weakness that can be exploited with advanced computing capability. An attacker who breaks the algorithm may use a MiTM position to decrypt the SSH tunnel and obtain credentials and information.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep -i "MACs"

rules.title: SSH idle timeout interval is configured
rules.explanation: The ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters control SSH session timeouts. When the ClientAliveInterval variable is set, ssh sessions that have no activity for the specified period of time are terminated. When the ClientAliveCountMax variable is set, sshd will send client alive messages at each ClientAliveInterval. When the number of consecutive client alive messages is sent without a response from the client, the ssh session is terminated.
rules.impact: The absence of a timeout value associated with a connection may allow an unauthorized user to access another user's ssh session (for example, a user leaves their computer and does not lock the screen). Setting a timeout value at least reduces this risk.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep clientaliveinterval

rules.title: SSH idle timeout interval is configured
rules.explanation: The ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters control SSH session timeouts. When the ClientAliveInterval variable is set, ssh sessions that have no activity for the specified period of time are terminated. When the ClientAliveCountMax variable is set, sshd will send client alive messages at each ClientAliveInterval. When the number of consecutive client alive messages is sent without a response from the client, the ssh session is terminated.
rules.impact: The absence of a timeout value associated with a connection may allow an unauthorized user to access another user's ssh session (for example, a user leaves their computer and does not lock the screen). Setting a timeout value at least reduces this risk.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep clientalivecountmax

rules.title: SSH LoginGraceTime is set to one minute or less
rules.explanation: The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication to the SSH server. The longer the grace period, the more unauthenticated connections may remain open. As with other session controls in this section, the grace period should be limited according to organizational constraints to ensure service availability for required access.
rules.impact: Setting a smaller value for LoginGraceTime minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. It also limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep logingracetime

rules.title: SSH warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted. By default, no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users of the site-specific policy regarding connection. Presenting a warning message before the user's normal login can help in the prosecution of computer system violators.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep banner

rules.title: Password creation requirements is configured
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality.so module checks password strength. It verifies that the password is not a dictionary word, has a specified length, contains a set of character classes (for example, letters, digits, and so on), and more. pam_pwquality.so parameter definitions: try_first_pass - obtain the password from the previous stacked PAM module. If it is unavailable, prompt the user for a password; retry = 3 - allow 3 attempts before returning an error. The following parameters are set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf: minlen = 14 - the password must be at least 14 characters including a special character.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect systems from brute-force attacks.

rules.title: Password reuse restrictions
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file stores users' old passwords and can be used to verify that users are not reusing recent passwords.
rules.impact: Preventing users from reusing their last 5 passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password.

rules.title: The password hashing algorithm is SHA-512 is configured
rules.explanation: The commands below change password hashing from md5 to sha512 (a much stronger hashing algorithm). All existing accounts will need to change their password to update stored hashes to the new algorithm.
rules.impact: The SHA-512 algorithm provides much stronger hashing than MD5, which provides additional system protection by increasing the effort required for an attacker to successfully determine passwords.

rules.title: Password lifetime does not exceed 365 days
rules.explanation: The PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to prevent users from changing their password until a minimum number of days have elapsed since the user's last password change.
rules.impact: The time during which an attacker can use compromised credentials, or successfully compromise credentials using an online brute-force attack, is limited by password age. Therefore, reducing the maximum password lifetime also reduces the attacker's window of opportunity.

rules.title: The minimum number of days between password changes is 7 or more
rules.explanation: The PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to prevent users from changing their password until a minimum number of days have elapsed since the user last changed their password.
rules.impact: By limiting password-change frequency, an administrator can prevent users from repeatedly changing their password in an attempt to bypass password-reuse controls.

rules.title: Password expiration warning period
rules.explanation: The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs allows the administrator to notify users that their password will expire in a specified number of days.
rules.impact: Advance warning that a password is about to expire gives users time to consider a strong password.

rules.title: Lock inactive passwords
rules.explanation: User accounts that have been inactive for a specified period can be automatically disabled.

rules.title: Default user umask value
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine the access permissions of newly created directories and files. In Linux, the default permissions for any newly created directory are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx), and for any newly created file are 0666 (rw-rw-rw-). Umask modifies the default Linux permissions by restricting (masking) those permissions. Users who want their files and directories to be readable by other users by default may choose a different default umask by inserting a umask command into the standard shell configuration files (.profile, .bashrc, etc.) in their home directories.
rules.impact: Setting a secure default umask ensures that users make a conscious choice regarding file access permissions. A permissive umask value can result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written by unauthorized users.

rules.title: User shell timeout
rules.explanation: TMOUT by default defines the shell idle timeout for users. The TMOUT value is measured in seconds.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized access to another user's shell session that has been left unattended. It also terminates an idle session and frees resources associated with that session.

rules.title: The local login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation:
The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log in on local terminals.
Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at login. This information may be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following options, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.

Authorized users can easily obtain this information by running the command "uname -a" after logging on.

rules.impact: Audit events must be captured for processes that start before audit so that potentially malicious activity cannot go unnoticed.

rules.title: The audit_backlog_limit parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel-level audit subsystem uses a socket buffer queue to store audit events. Whenever a new audit event arrives, it is recorded and prepared for addition to this queue. The kernel boot parameter audit_backlog_limit=N, where N represents the number of messages, ensures that the queue cannot grow beyond a certain size. If an audit event is recorded that would cause the queue to exceed this limit, a failure occurs that is handled according to the system configuration.
rules.impact: If an audit event is recorded that causes the queue to grow beyond audit_backlog_limit, a failure occurs, audit records are lost, and potentially malicious activity may go unnoticed.

rules.title: Auditd rules for system date and time changes are configured
rules.explanation: Capture events when the system date and/or time were changed.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to the system date and/or time may be an indication of malicious activity on the system.

rules.title: Events that change user or group information are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: Record events that affect changes to user or group information, including passwords and old passwords if they are used.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes in these files may indicate that the system has been compromised and that an unauthorized user is attempting to hide their activity or compromise additional accounts.

rules.title: Login and logout events are monitored is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor logon and logoff events.
rules.impact: Monitoring logon/logoff events can provide the system administrator with information related to attacks against user logon.

rules.title: Changes to files related to session events are audited is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor session initiation events. The parameters in this section track changes to files associated with session events.
rules.impact: Monitoring these files for changes can alert a system administrator to logons at unusual times, which may indicate attacker activity (that is, a user logging on at a time when they do not normally log on).

rules.title: Auditd rules for programs with setuid and/or setgid are configured
rules.explanation: Monitor privileged programs that have the setuid and/or setgid bit set on execution to determine whether unprivileged users are executing these commands.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to the system date and/or time may be an indication of malicious activity on the system.

rules.title: System calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes are audited is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor use of system calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes.
rules.impact: Tracking these calls from unprivileged users can provide the system administrator with evidence that improper deletion of files and file attributes associated with protected files is occurring. Although this audit option will capture all events, system administrators will want to look for specific privileged files that are deleted or modified.

rules.title: Auditd rules for sudoers are configured
rules.explanation: Monitor scope changes for system administrators. If the system has been correctly configured to force system administrators to log in as themselves first and then use the sudo command to execute privileged commands, scope changes can be monitored. The /etc/sudoers file or files in /etc/sudoers.d will be written when the files or related attributes are changed. Audit records will be tagged with the identifier "scope".
rules.impact: Changes to /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d may indicate that an unauthorized change was made to the system administrator's scope of activity.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Rsyslog software is recommended in environments where journald does not meet operational requirements.
rules.impact: Rsyslog security improvements, such as connection-oriented log transport (that is, TCP), the ability to log in database format, and encryption of log data in transit to a central log server, justify installing and configuring the package.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host private key files are configured
rules.explanation: The SSH private key is one of the two files used in SSH public-key authentication. In this authentication method, possession of the private key is confirmation of identity. Only the private key that corresponds to the public key will authenticate successfully. Private keys must be stored and handled carefully, and copies of the private key must not be distributed.
rules.impact: If an unauthorized user obtains the SSH host private key file, the host may be compromised.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host public key files are configured
rules.explanation: An SSH public key is one of two files used in SSH public key authentication. In this authentication method, the public key is the key that can be used to verify digital signatures generated using the corresponding private key. Only the public key corresponding to the private key will be able to successfully authenticate.
rules.impact: If the host public key file is modified by an unauthorized user, the SSH service may be compromised.

rules.title: System accounts are secured is configured
rules.explanation: Most distributions include a number of accounts used to manage applications that are not intended to provide an interactive shell.
rules.impact: It is important to Ensure that accounts not used by regular users cannot be used to provide an interactive shell. By default, most distributions set an invalid string in the password field for these accounts, but it is also recommended that the shell field in the password file be set to the nologin shell. This prevents the account from potentially being used to run any commands.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo, which provides more granular control over privileged access. Typically, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in /etc/pam.d/su, the su command will allow only users in specified groups to execute su. This group should be empty to reinforce the use of sudo for privileged access.
rules.impact: Restricting use of su and using sudo instead gives system administrators better control over user privilege elevation for privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and auditing mechanism because it can log every command executed via sudo, whereas su can record only that the user executed the su program.

rules.title: Integrity of the root PATH is configured
rules.explanation: The root user can execute any command on the system and can be tricked into unintentionally executing programs if PATH is not set correctly.
rules.impact: Including the current working directory (.) or another writable directory in the root executable path increases the likelihood that an attacker can obtain superuser access by causing an administrator running as root to execute a Trojan program.

rules.title: Users' dot files are not group- or world-writable is configured
rules.explanation: Although a system administrator can set secure permissions on users' dot files, users can easily override them.
rules.impact: Group-writable or world-writable user configuration files can allow attackers to steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although the useradd program will not allow you to create a duplicate user identifier (UID), an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the UID field.
rules.impact: Users must be assigned unique UIDs for accountability and to ensure proper access protection.

rules.title: No duplicate usernames exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although useradd will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: No duplicate usernames exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although useradd will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although groupadd will not allow you to create a duplicate group name, an administrator can manually edit /etc/group and change a group name.
rules.impact: If a group is assigned a duplicate group name, it will create and access files with the first GID for that group in /etc/group. Essentially, the GID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: The shadow group is empty is configured
rules.explanation: The shadow group allows system programs that require read access to /etc/shadow. Users must not be assigned to the shadow group.
rules.impact: All users assigned to the shadow group will be granted read access to /etc/shadow. If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/shadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed passwords to crack them. Other security information stored in /etc/shadow (for example, expiration dates) may also be useful for compromising additional user accounts.

rules.title: Wi-Fi is disabled on the OS
rules.explanation: The operating system includes a set of wireless networking tools that allow system administrators to configure and use wireless networks.
rules.impact: If wireless communication is not used, wireless devices can be disabled to reduce a potential attack vector.

rules.title: SSH PAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface. If set to "yes", this will enable PAM authentication using the ChallengeResponseAuthentication and PasswordAuthentication directives in addition to PAM account and session module processing for all authentication types.
rules.impact: If the usePAM parameter is set to yes, PAM correctly works with account and session types. This is important if you want to restrict access to services based on IP, time, or other account factors. In addition, you can ensure that users inherit certain environment variables at logon or deny access to the server.

rules.title: Prohibit mounting of cramfs filesystems
rules.explanation: The cramfs file system type is a compressed read-only Linux file system used in embedded systems with limited memory. A cramfs image can be used without first decompressing it.
rules.impact: Disabling support for unnecessary filesystem types reduces the likelihood of attack. If this filesystem type is not required, it should be disabled.

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition is configured
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is world-writable and is used for temporary data storage by all users and some applications.
rules.impact: Creating /tmp as a separate filesystem allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec, making /tmp useless to an attacker attempting to introduce executable code.

rules.title: The nodev option is set for the /var partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because /var is not intended to support devices, this option prevents the creation of block or character devices on this partition.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set for the /var partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid option prohibits use of setuid files in the file system.
rules.impact: Because /var is intended for variable files (for example, logs), this option prevents creation of potentially dangerous executables with elevated privileges.

rules.title: The nodev option is set for the /var/log partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev option prevents the use of special devices on the filesystem.
rules.impact: The /var/log partition is intended only for log storage, so device files are not required there and may be dangerous.

rules.title: The noexec option is set for the /var/log partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec option prevents execution of programs on this partition.
rules.impact: Because /var/log contains only logs, executable files are not needed there and their presence could be used for attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set for the /var/log partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid option disables the use of setuid files.
rules.impact: Logs must not contain executable files with elevated privileges, as this may lead to privilege escalation.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/log/audit partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev option prevents device creation on the partition.
rules.impact: Audit logs should not contain devices, as this can be used to bypass access control.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/log/audit partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec option prohibits code execution on this partition.
rules.impact: Audit logs must not contain executable files, to prevent execution of malicious code.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/log/audit partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid option disables setuid files on the partition.
rules.impact: Audit logs must not contain files with elevated privileges, as this may lead to privilege escalation.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set for the /home partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid option prohibits the use of setuid files in user home directories.
rules.impact: Users must not be able to create executable files with elevated privileges in their home directories.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Package repositories contain software updates and security patches.
rules.impact: Correct repository configuration ensures that the system receives current and secure updates.

rules.title: GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: GPG keys are used to verify package authenticity.
rules.impact: Package signature verification prevents installation of modified or malicious software.

rules.title: Ptrace_scope is restricted
rules.explanation: The ptrace utility allows process debugging but may be abused by attackers.
rules.impact: Restricting ptrace reduces the risk of attacks that interfere with processes.

rules.title: Prohibit automatic sending of error reports
rules.explanation: Automatic error reports may transmit sensitive data.
rules.impact: Disabling this feature prevents information leakage.

rules.title: Remove GNOME Display Manager (GDM)
rules.explanation: GDM is the graphical login manager for GNOME.
rules.impact: If GDM is not used, removing it reduces the likelihood of attack.

rules.title: The disable-user-list option in GDM is enabled
rules.explanation: This option hides the user list on the logon screen.
rules.impact: Hiding the user list makes credential guessing more difficult.

rules.title: GDM screen lock on idle is configured
rules.explanation: The screen must lock after a period of inactivity.
rules.impact: This prevents unauthorized access if the user steps away.

rules.title: Prohibit canceling GDM screen lock
rules.explanation: Users must not be able to override the screen lock.
rules.impact: This makes bypassing protections more difficult.

rules.title: Automatic mounting of removable media in GDM is disabled
rules.explanation: USB device automounting can be dangerous.
rules.impact: This reduces the risk of executing malicious code from removable media.

rules.title: Prohibit overriding the disablement of automount in GDM
rules.explanation: Users must not be able to enable automounting.
rules.impact: Maintaining a stable security configuration.

rules.title: The autorun-never option in GDM is enabled
rules.explanation: This option prevents autorun of removable media contents.
rules.impact: Prevents execution of malicious code when devices are connected.

rules.title: Prohibit overriding autorun-never in GDM
rules.explanation: Users must not be able to disable this option.
rules.impact: Provides persistent protection against autorun.

rules.title: XDMCP is disabled
rules.explanation: XDCMP allows remote control of X11 sessions.
rules.impact: Disabling this prevents potential remote access attacks.

rules.title: Only one time synchronization daemon is used is configured
rules.explanation: The system should use only one time-synchronization daemon (NTP, chrony, or systemd-timesyncd). Having multiple daemons running concurrently may cause conflicts and incorrect system operation.
rules.impact: Using multiple time-synchronization daemons can cause conflicts in system operation and result in incorrect time, which can affect applications that depend on accurate time, such as authentication and logging systems.

rules.title: Chrony is configured with an authorized time server
rules.explanation: The chrony daemon must be configured to use trusted NTP servers specified in organizational policy.
rules.impact: Using untrusted or public NTP servers can result in forged timestamps, which can be used to attack authentication systems and other services that depend on accurate time.

rules.title: Chrony is run as the _chrony user is configured
rules.explanation: The chrony daemon should run under the dedicated unprivileged user _chrony, not as root.
rules.impact: Running the service as an unprivileged user reduces the risk of exploiting potential vulnerabilities in chrony for privilege escalation on the system.

rules.title: Systemd-timesyncd is configured with an authorized time server
rules.explanation: The systemd-timesyncd service must be configured to use trusted NTP servers specified in organizational policy.
rules.impact: Using untrusted time servers can result in timestamp manipulation, which can affect system security.

rules.title: NTP access control is configured
rules.explanation: The NTP server must be configured with access restrictions to prevent unauthorized queries and time modifications.
rules.impact: Without proper access controls, attackers can manipulate server time or use an NTP server for amplification DDoS attacks.

rules.title: NTP is configured with an authorized time server
rules.explanation: NTP must be configured to synchronize only with trusted NTP servers specified in organizational policy.
rules.impact: Using untrusted time servers can result in timestamp spoofing and disruption of systems that depend on accurate time.

rules.title: NTP runs as the ntp user is configured
rules.explanation: The NTP daemon must run as the dedicated unprivileged ntp user, not as root.
rules.impact: Running the service as an unprivileged user reduces the risk of exploiting NTP vulnerabilities for privilege escalation on the system.

rules.title: Avahi server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The Avahi service (an mDNS/DNS-SD implementation) should not be installed on the system unless required for operation.
rules.impact: Avahi may disclose information about the system and services that adversaries can use for reconnaissance.

rules.title: CUPS is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The CUPS print server must not be installed unless required for operations.
rules.impact: CUPS may contain vulnerabilities and increase the likelihood of a system attack.

rules.title: DHCP server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The DHCP server (isc-dhcp-server) must not be installed unless required for operations.
rules.impact: An unauthorized DHCP server can disrupt network operations and be used for man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.title: LDAP server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The LDAP server (slapd) must not be installed unless required for operations.
rules.impact: An unsecured LDAP server may disclose sensitive information and be used for attacks.

rules.title: NFS is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The NFS server (nfs-kernel-server) must not be installed unless required for operations.
rules.impact: NFS is vulnerable to attacks if not configured properly and may expose file systems.

rules.title: The absence of IMAP and POP3 servers is configured
rules.explanation: IMAP and POP3 servers (dovecot-imapd, dovecot-pop3d) should not be installed unless required for operation.
rules.impact: These protocols are obsolete and vulnerable to attacks if not configured properly.

rules.title: Dnsmasq is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The dnsmasq DNS server must not be installed unless required for operations.
rules.impact: An unauthorized DNS server may be used for "DNS cache poisoning" attacks.

rules.title: The rsync service is not installed or is masked is configured
rules.explanation: The rsync service must not be active unless required for operations.
rules.impact: Rsync may expose files if configured incorrectly.

rules.title: RPC is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The RPC service (rpcbind) must not be installed unless required for operations.
rules.impact: RPC is vulnerable to remote attacks and may disclose system information.

rules.title: Unnecessary services are removed or disabled is configured
rules.explanation: All unused services must be removed or disabled.
rules.impact: Each active service increases the likelihood of a system attack.

rules.title: The IPv6 status is defined is configured
rules.explanation: IPv6 is a newer version of the Internet Protocol that complements IPv4. Determining the IPv6 status helps establish whether it is in use on the system.
rules.impact: Understanding IPv6 status allows network security to be configured correctly and avoids potential vulnerabilities associated with misconfiguration.

rules.title: Bluetooth is disabled
rules.explanation: Bluetooth is a wireless communication technology that may pose a security threat if it is not in use.
rules.impact: Disabling Bluetooth reduces the risk of unauthorized system access through vulnerabilities in wireless interfaces.

rules.title: Iptables-persistent is not installed together with ufw is configured
rules.explanation: Ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall) and iptables-persistent are two different tools for managing the firewall. Using them together can lead to conflicts.
rules.impact: Using a single tool to manage the firewall simplifies configuration and reduces the risk of misconfiguration.

rules.title: Ufw is removed or disabled when using nftables is configured
rules.explanation: Nftables is a modern replacement for iptables, and concurrent use of ufw may result in conflicts.
rules.impact: Using only one tool to manage the firewall ensures system stability and security.

rules.title: Nftables is not installed together with iptables is configured
rules.explanation: Iptables and nftables are two different tools for managing the firewall, and using them together is not recommended.
rules.impact: Using only one tool prevents conflicts and simplifies firewall management.

rules.title: Ufw is removed or disabled when using iptables is configured
rules.explanation: Iptables and ufw perform similar functions, and using them together may cause conflicts.
rules.impact: Using only one tool ensures consistency and security of the firewall configuration.

rules.title: Users must provide a password to elevate privileges is configured
rules.explanation: Requiring a password when using sudo increases security by preventing unauthorized privilege elevation.
rules.impact: This reduces the risk of abuse of privileged commands if a user account is compromised.

rules.title: Re-authentication for privilege elevation is not disabled globally is configured
rules.explanation: Reauthentication ensures that the user confirms their identity when performing privileged operations.
rules.impact: This prevents session abuse if the user temporarily leaves the workstation.

rules.title: The sudo authentication timeout is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The timestamp_timeout parameter in the sudo configuration defines the period of time (in minutes) during which a user can execute privileged commands without re-entering a password.
rules.impact: An excessively long timeout increases the risk of unauthorized access if the user leaves a session unattended. The recommended value is 5–15 minutes.

rules.title: All current passwords use the configured hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: The system must use modern password hashing algorithms (for example, SHA-512 instead of obsolete MD5 or DES).
rules.impact: Weak algorithms are vulnerable to brute-force attacks. SHA-512 provides cryptographic strength and meets modern security standards.

rules.title: The minimum number of changed characters in a new password is configured
rules.explanation: Password policy should require a specified number of characters to change (for example, 8 of 10) when a password is changed.
rules.impact: Prevents the use of slightly modified old passwords (for example, "Password1" ? "Password2").

rules.title: Dictionary words are prohibited in passwords is configured
rules.explanation: Passwords must not contain simple dictionary words (for example, "admin", "password") that are easy to guess.
rules.impact: Reduces the risk of successful dictionary attacks.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shells file contains the list of allowed shells for user logon. The nologin shell (which denies logon) should not be in this list.
rules.impact: The presence of nologin in /etc/shells may result in unintended user lockouts.

rules.title: The maximum number of identical consecutive characters in a password is configured
rules.explanation: Passwords must not contain repeating characters (for example, "aaaaaa" or "111111").
rules.impact: Such passwords are easily susceptible to brute-force attacks.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote is installed is configured
rules.explanation: The systemd-journal-remote package provides functionality for receiving and forwarding event logs between systems.
rules.impact: Provides centralized logging and secure log transmission.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote is configured
rules.explanation: Configure settings for secure receipt and forwarding of logs.
rules.impact: Proper configuration ensures reliable and secure log transmission.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote is enabled
rules.explanation: The service must be enabled for automatic startup.
rules.impact: Ensures continuous operation of the log forwarding service.

rules.title: Journald is not configured to receive logs from remote clients is configured
rules.explanation: The systemd journal must not accept data from remote systems.
rules.impact: Reduces the risk of unauthorized access to logs.

rules.title: Journald is not configured to send logs to rsyslog is configured
rules.explanation: Forwarding logs to rsyslog should be disabled.
rules.impact: Prevents log duplication and potential conflicts.

rules.title: Journald log rotation is configured according to site policy
rules.explanation: Configure log rotation settings to manage log size and retention.
rules.impact: Prevents disk overflow and ensures logs are retained in accordance with requirements.

rules.title: Permissions on journald log files are configured correctly
rules.explanation: Set strict permissions on log files.
rules.impact: Protects logs from unauthorized access.

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to receive logs from remote clients is configured
rules.explanation: Rsyslog must not accept logs from remote systems unless required.
rules.impact: Reduces the risk of unauthorized access and attacks.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: Audit security context changes using chcon.
rules.impact: Allows tracking of file security context changes.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: Audit ACL changes using setfacl.
rules.impact: Allows tracking of file permission changes.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: Audit ACL changes using chacl.
rules.impact: Allows tracking of file permission changes.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: Audit user account changes using usermod.
rules.impact: Allows tracking of user account changes.

rules.title: The current and saved audit configurations match is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that the current audit configuration matches the saved configuration.
rules.impact: Ensures that changes to the audit configuration have been applied correctly.

rules.title: Audit configuration files have permissions of 640 or more restrictive is configured
rules.explanation: Set strict permissions on audit configuration files.
rules.impact: Protects audit configuration from unauthorized access.

rules.title: Audit configuration files are owned by root is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files must be owned by the root user.
rules.impact: Provides control over the audit configuration.

rules.title: Audit configuration files are owned by the root group is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files must be owned by the root group.
rules.impact: Restricts access to audit configuration.

rules.title: Audit tools have permissions of 755 or more restrictive is configured
rules.explanation: Set strict access permissions on audit tools.
rules.impact: Protects audit tools from unauthorized access.

rules.title: Audit tools are owned by the root user is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools must be owned by the root user.
rules.impact: Provides control over audit tools.

rules.title: Audit tools are owned by the root group is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools must be owned by the root group.
rules.impact: Restricts access to audit tools.

rules.title: Cryptographic mechanisms are used to protect the integrity of audit tools is configured
rules.explanation: Use hashes (for example, SHA-256) to verify the integrity of audit tools.
rules.impact: Protects audit tools from modification.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shells are configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/shells file contains a list of valid login shells. Strict access permissions must be set on this file.
rules.impact: Restricting permissions prevents unauthorized modification of the list of allowed shells, which could lead to use of insecure shells.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/opasswd are configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/opasswd file (if it exists) stores old password hashes. Access to this file must be restricted.
rules.impact: Protects older password hashes from unauthorized access, reducing the risk of brute-force attacks.

rules.title: Accounts in /etc/passwd use shadow passwords is configured
rules.explanation: All passwords must be stored in the /etc/shadow file, not in /etc/passwd. /etc/passwd must contain x instead of password hashes.
rules.impact: The /etc/passwd file is readable by all users, while /etc/shadow is readable only by root. This prevents theft of password hashes.

rules.title: Access to local interactive user dotfiles is configured correctly
rules.explanation: Dot files (for example, ~/.bashrc, ~/.ssh/) must have strict permissions that deny write access for the group and other users.
rules.impact: Protects user configuration files from modification by attackers.
